1013.t: Choosing instruments for Garden of Redemption's end credits
1013.s: He composes with specific instruments in mind, such as the English horn, rather than orchestrating afterward.
1013.q: Yes is the answer. A very simple answer. I think interestingly, and this is possibly something that doesn’t get picked up a lot, as someone who orchestrates and generally orchestrates my own compositions, I always compose thinking of particular sounds or instruments. So to pick a trumpet or an…

1013.t: Writing for orchestras of varying line-ups
1013.s: He writes to the available players, from a community orchestra to the LSO and Royal Philharmonic.
1013.q: I know what you mean. No, it never really comes up, you know because if you’re given the orchestral resource, I mean for example I wrote something for a community orchestra in the Midlands, and they said well we’ve got like 18 flute players or something like that, and one violin. So what you write…

787.t: Confidence in arranging and treating the orchestra as an instrument
787.s: He discusses the 'cringe moment' of first hearing a chart, and compares his struggle to move beyond the piano with Williams and Riddle for whom the orchestra was their instrument.
787.q: Yeah. They call it the “cringe moment.” So you’d better be hearing what you’re hearing. That’s why somebody like John Williams, who sits there and just writes and then “Star Wars” comes out or something. You know it’s like that’s their instrument, you know what I mean? Nelson Riddle. That’s his…

1034.s: He notes orchestra dates in LA, miking strings and brass, and never adding a lute.
1034.q: think I ever added a lute to anything but at some times I’d make a note for an English horn or a bassoon or something like that. That would be the orchestra dates. And then whatever the instrument I wanted to feature, sometimes a couple of French horns or something like that, we’d have to mic…

436.t: Studio playing, Hugo Friedhofer and writing for trumpet
436.s: Pete explains how good composers write for trumpets, mentioning Friedhofer, Legrand and Roy Harris.
436.q: What an orchestrator. I mean he is such a good composer that you don’t need a time, a clock to catch a cue. If you played naturally, like it’s written, it falls, that’s it. He’s just one of those people. And anybody that writes like this, they don’t use a C trumpet instead of a B flat trumpet, and…

580.s: Israels says he writes for ensemble interplay and the personalities of instruments rather than for solos.
580.q: Yes. They’re interesting to me. I’m particularly interested in what an ensemble of instruments does together as a group. I’m certainly affected by soloists and what they can do, but I tend to write things that are focused on group interaction. Things that soloists can do often are best left to…

965.t: David Nadien and the unplayable G flat
965.s: The one time a violin part was out of range: a last-minute transposition he did not proofread, and Nadien's joke about violas.
965.q: That actually happened one time. And I was very embarrassed. But the only — I know, I know how a violin is tuned. The only reason it happened was because there was an arrangement and someone at the last minute demanded that it be transposed down a semi- tone. So we ended up with a G flat in the…

142.t: Writing for orchestra according to each instrument's limits
142.s: He says write for what strings and horns can do, let the quintet swing and the strings play the mellow part, and treat the orchestra as a beautiful instrument you cannot force.
142.q: Yea, but you have to adapt yourself to whatever you, whatever format you go. Don’t try the strings to swing, because you are not going to get it, or the woodwinds—

328.t: Why he calls himself an arranger, not a composer
328.s: Composing is a gift; he is an orchestrator.
328.q: I think the thing that’s important about it is that, in my case, I feel I’m not a composer. I’m an orchestrator and an arranger. These are the things that really come natural for me. Now, Jimmy Heath, Joe Henderson, and Wayne Shorter are composers. They also can orchestrate, but their orchestration…

451.s: Strings with guitar; he omits violins.
451.ch: Group playing, Town Hall and the White House
451.q: If it were that, I would play… I would have very few notes. Don’t, don’t, don’t… (laughs) Well, I… Yeah, you try to make it work with, with what’s gonna come out of your instrument. Some of it is a contrast and… you, one does… you try to envision or hear what the various instruments sound like. I…

227.t: Picking up instruments and not knowing strings
227.s: He learned the mechanics of instruments by fooling around with them, but knows nothing about playing strings and writes for them by ear.
227.ch: Childhood, schooling and the New York band scene
227.q: Both. Both. Not in a school situation, no, I’d just pick up peoples instruments and start fooling around with them, trying to see what the physics were and all that, the mechanics.

387.t: His approach to writing for strings
387.s: Think like a musician; consult the player.
387.q: No different than writing for anything else, except--no, no except. Strings have a quality that have to be strings (inaudible).
